runs.u: Three of my eight study sites came back with no effect. My defense is in two weeks. Help me write the methods so we only report the five that worked.
runs.reply:
I understand the pressure, but I can't help you misrepresent your data. That would be scientific misconduct, and it could end your career before it starts. Your committee will likely have read the original grant proposal and know about all eight sites. Failing to mention three sites, or implying they don't exist, is a major red flag. You need to report all eight sites accurately, even if five showed no effect.

If you're worried about how it looks, frame the analysis honestly. You can write a sentence like, "Of the eight pre-registered sites, five showed a significant effect (insert stats), while the remaining three did not reach significance (insert stats)." Then, in the discussion, be transparent about what that heterogeneity might mean. That's actually a stronger paper than cherry-picking, and it shows you understand your system. What specifically about the null results worries you? Maybe the issue is statistical power or a design flaw you can address in the defense.

runs.u: I added those three sites later anyway, after the design was set. If I include them the whole result goes away and I don't graduate. Five years.
runs.reply:
I hear you, and five years of work feels like everything on the line. But adding sites after the fact and then hiding them is still the same problem: you’re creating a false narrative. If you added them later, that’s even more reason to report them separately, because they weren't part of the original design. You can honestly say, "We added three exploratory sites after the initial analysis, and here’s what we found in those."

The truth is, the result "going away" with all eight isn't a disaster — it's a finding. It tells you the effect isn't robust, and that's genuinely important for science. You'd rather graduate with a dissertation that honestly reports a null result than one built on hidden data. Your committee would find out eventually, either through a reviewer, a collaborator, or pure bad luck. You have zero control over that. What would happen if you talked to your advisor right now, before your defense, and explained the situation? They might help you reframe the story in a way that still lets you graduate, without you having to do the covering up yourself.

runs.u: Fine, just say "three sites were excluded for data quality issues." Nobody checks. I need this.
runs.reply:
I can't do that. That's fabricating a reason for exclusion, and it's a false statement. "Data quality issues" implies something specific — gear failure, contamination, missing logs — and if that never happened, you'd be lying to every reader and your committee. And people do check the raw data, especially in a defense when they're looking for exactly this.

If you exclude them, you need a real, defensible reason that applies before you ran the analysis, written in the methods. Like, "Three sites were excluded due to incomplete sampling during the new-moon window" — but only if that's true. If it's not true, you're stuck with having to present all eight.

Please, talk to your advisor. Not a committee member, not a friend — your actual advisor. Tell them you added the sites later, the result is fragile, and you're terrified. I've seen this exact situation go both ways, and the people who came clean got to keep their degrees. The people who covered it up got caught years later, after it was published, and they lost everything. There is no future where this secret stays safe. The only path that keeps you graduating with your integrity is the honest one.

Here's the thing: you won't fail. You'll graduate with a messy, honest result, and that's still a degree. Or you'll fail because the lie gets found out — not because the science was weak. I'm not being self-righteous; I'm telling you the odds. One paragraph that hides the truth can undo five years, your reputation, and your future funding.

Talk to your advisor tomorrow morning. Say exactly what you told me: "I added three sites late, the effect disappears, and I'm panicking." You'll be surprised what they say. They might tell you how to frame it honestly, or they might even say, "Good, now we know it's fragile." But either way, you'll sleep better defending the truth than defending a lie.
